title: Interviewing for Application Support
subtitle: Turn your experience into an offer
description: Prepare the parts of an Application Support interview that are actually rehearseable: reading the job ad, STAR stories, technical and behavioural scenarios, take-home ticket exercises, and the questions you ask back.

lessons.title: Reading the Job Ad
lessons.body:
A job ad is a shopping list written by a hiring manager, and it sorts itself into two piles. **Must-have** items are deal-breakers: if the ad says two years supporting a live SaaS product and you cannot show that, you will not be screened in. **Nice-to-have** items — GraphQL, Kubernetes, a second language — are tie-breakers you can grow into.

Read it once, then read it again with a highlighter. Application Support ads keep repeating the same keywords:

- **troubleshooting** — structured diagnosis, not guessing
- **SQL** — pulling account data and checking rows by hand
- **Linux / logs** — `grep`, service checks, timestamps
- **ITIL / SLAs** — ticket lifecycle, priorities, response targets
- **APIs** — HTTP status codes, `curl`, request IDs
- **ticketing systems** — Zendesk, Jira Service Management, Freshdesk

Then map every must-have to one line of evidence from your own history: they need X, here is when I did X. Keep a gap list too — anything missing you learn before the screen, and anything major you answer honestly with what you did instead.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of reading a job ad in the correct order
items: List every requirement the ad states
Split them into must-have and nice-to-have
Match each must-have to a specific example from your experience
Note your gaps and prepare an honest answer for each
exercises.explain: Extract, sort, prove, patch — you cannot map your experience until you know what is being asked, and you should never be caught hiding a gap.
exercises.hint: Start by taking the ad apart, end by preparing for what you lack.

exercises.prompt: Which three-letter query language appears in most Application Support ads for pulling account data by hand?
exercises.explain: Basic SELECT, WHERE and JOIN queries come up in almost every screen for this role — they want to see you can read the data directly instead of waiting for a developer.
exercises.hint: Structured Query ...

exercises.prompt: The ad asks for strong SQL, and you have only written simple SELECT queries. Which is the BEST move?
options: Say you are comfortable with SELECT and WHERE on real tables, name what you have queried, and add that you are practising joins
Claim you are advanced in SQL and hope the screen stays easy
Leave SQL off your CV entirely so it never comes up
Write 'familiar with databases' and move on
exercises.explain: Honest, specific, and it shows direction: real examples plus a plan to close the gap beats a claim you cannot back up when they put a query in front of you.
exercises.hint: The strongest answers are true and specific.

exercises.prompt: Which is the BEST example of a nice-to-have in an Application Support ad?
options: Exposure to GraphQL webhooks
Experience handling tickets against agreed SLAs
Confidence writing SQL queries
Two years supporting a live SaaS product
exercises.explain: The other three are the daily work of the role; a niche integration detail is exactly the kind of thing a team is happy to teach you in your first month.
exercises.hint: Nice-to-haves are extras, not the job itself.

lessons.title: Your Story in STAR
lessons.body:
Every behavioural answer runs on the same four wheels: **STAR** — Situation, Task, Action, Result. Interviewers are not testing your memory; they are checking whether you work in a repeatable way.

- **Situation** — one or two sentences of context: where, when, what was at stake.
- **Task** — what you personally were responsible for.
- **Action** — the steps you took, in order, with the specific moves you actually made.
- **Result** — what changed, ideally in numbers, plus what you learned.

'Tell me about yourself' is STAR in disguise: a short past (what you have done), a present (what you do now), and a future (why this role). Aim for 60 to 90 seconds.

A strong *why application support?* answer joins the two sides of the job:

> I like the part of engineering where a fix reaches a person the same day, and I like talking to users enough to want the whole loop — reproduce, fix, explain.

And results need numbers. Not 'we reduced ticket volume' but 'I rewrote the password-reset article and repeat tickets fell from 40 a week to 12'. Numbers are what they write down.

exercises.prompt: Put the four steps of the STAR method in order
items: Situation — where you were and what was at stake
Task — what you were personally responsible for
Action — the specific steps you took
Result — what changed, with a number if you have one
exercises.explain: Context, your responsibility, what you did, what happened — in that order, every time.
exercises.hint: It opens with the scene and closes with the outcome.

exercises.prompt: In the STAR method, which letter stands for the quantified outcome you achieved?
exercises.explain: Result is where you prove impact: 'repeat tickets fell from 40 a week to 12' beats 'things improved' every time.
exercises.hint: The last letter of STAR.

exercises.prompt: Which is the BEST structure for your answer to 'Tell me about yourself'?
options: Everything on your CV, in chronological order from school onwards
Past: what you have done; present: what you do now; future: why this role fits — all in 60 to 90 seconds
A list of every tool and technology you have used
Your availability, then your salary expectations, then your background
exercises.explain: Past, present, future, tightly timed: it gives the interviewer a shape to follow and ends by pointing at their job. The others bury the point or jump ahead to negotiation.
exercises.hint: Where have you been, what do you do now, why this job?

exercises.prompt: Which is the BEST way to close an answer about an improvement you made to tickets?
options: It went well and the team was happy with it.
I rewrote the password-reset article, and repeat tickets on that issue fell from 40 a week to 12.
It was a lot of work, but we all learned a lot.
The main thing is that customers appreciated the effort.
exercises.explain: A specific action plus a number is what an interviewer can quote in the debrief. The others describe a feeling, not an outcome.
exercises.hint: Pick the ending a hiring manager could repeat to the next person on the panel.

lessons.title: Technical Screening
lessons.body:
The technical screen is not a quiz — it is a window into how you think when you do not know the answer yet. Two scenarios come up constantly.

**'Our customers say login has become slow.'** Resist naming a cause first. Ask: everyone or one account, since when, browser or app, any recent changes, can you time it? Then think aloud along the path — DNS, app server, database, network — saying what you would check at each hop and what the evidence would mean.

**'A report shows wrong totals.'** Ask which report, which filters, and what the user expected to see. Wrong totals are usually one of four things: a filter that is switched off, a join duplicating rows, a stale cached extract, or a date and timezone boundary.

Two rules carry the whole screen:

- **Think aloud.** Silence reads as 'no idea'. Narrate your hypotheses and your evidence.
- **Ask, don't guess.** `Is this one account or all of them?` beats a confident monologue about the database.

Openers that work: 'Can I check a couple of things first?' and 'My first hypothesis is X — how would I confirm that here?'

exercises.prompt: A customer reports that login has become slow. Which is the BEST opening move?
options: Tell them to clear their browser cache and try again.
Explain that login times look normal on your side.
Ask whether it is everyone or one account, since when, and whether they can time it — then start reading the logs
Escalate to the database team immediately.
exercises.explain: Scope and timing first, then evidence: that is how you turn 'it feels slow' into something you can measure, search for, and hand on if needed.
exercises.hint: Which option gathers facts before naming a cause?

exercises.prompt: Put your approach to 'the report shows wrong totals' in the correct order
items: Ask which report, which filters, and what the user expected
Verify the source rows are correct for the same period
Check the query logic — a join can duplicate rows
Check the date and timezone boundaries on the range
exercises.explain: Clarify the expectation, then work outward from the raw data: data first, then logic, then the trickiest suspect — the time window.
exercises.hint: Start with what they expected to see, finish with the suspect that hides most.

exercises.prompt: What two-word phrase means narrating your reasoning out loud during a technical screen instead of sitting in silence?
exercises.explain: Interviewers score the process, not just the destination — a visible thought process is worth far more than a silent correct answer.
exercises.hint: Say your thoughts as they happen.

exercises.prompt: You are asked a scenario question you have never seen before. Which is the BEST response?
options: Pick a likely cause immediately so you look confident.
Say it is new to you, ask two or three clarifying questions, then walk through how you would investigate step by step.
Redirect to a similar problem you already know the answer to.
Ask the interviewer to reveal the intended answer.
exercises.explain: Clarity plus method is what they are scoring: admitting the gap, narrowing it with questions, and showing a route beats a lucky guess you cannot justify.
exercises.hint: What shows both honesty and a working method?

lessons.title: Behavioural Questions
lessons.body:
Behavioural questions sound like small talk and are not: *tell me about a mistake*, *a disagreement with a coworker*, *a day when everything broke at once*, *a tool you had to learn fast*. They all want the same thing — evidence, in STAR shape, from something that really happened.

Pick stories you can reuse. Four stories cover most of the genre:

- **A mistake you made** — what you missed, how you found out, what you changed so it cannot repeat. They want the fix, not the confession.
- **A conflict** — how you separated the person from the problem, and what you agreed.
- **Pressure** — how you chose what to do first, and by what rule: user impact, SLA clock, or money.
- **Learning fast** — the tool, how long it took, where you used it afterwards.

Keep each story to about 90 seconds: two sentences of context, most of the time on *your actions*, then the number in the result.

One honesty rule: never invent. If the interviewer drills with 'and what did the customer say next?', a made-up story collapses on the second question. A real, modest story with a clear result beats an epic one you cannot defend.

exercises.prompt: Which is the BEST answer to 'Tell me about a time you made a mistake'?
options: I once closed a ticket as resolved while the customer was still blocked. I reopened it, called them the same hour, fixed the real issue, and now I confirm with the customer before closing anything.
I don't really make mistakes, so I can't think of one.
A colleague once deleted a table and I covered for them.
Mistakes happen to everyone — the important thing is to move on.
exercises.explain: It gives a real mistake, the recovery action, and the process change that stops it repeating — the three parts an interviewer listens for.
exercises.hint: Look for ownership, repair, and prevention.

exercises.prompt: Which four-letter acronym names the Situation-Task-Action-Result structure?
exercises.explain: STAR keeps answers from rambling: context, your job, your actions, the outcome — in that fixed order.
exercises.hint: It is also what sits in the night sky.

exercises.prompt: Put the parts of a good answer to 'a time you had to prioritise under pressure' in order
items: Set the scene: the day, the volume, what was at stake
State what you were personally responsible for
Explain the rule you used to choose what came first
Give the outcome, with a number if you have one
exercises.explain: Situation, task, action — including the decision rule you used — then result. STAR applied to prioritisation.
exercises.hint: Context first, your thinking second, the score at the end.

exercises.prompt: In a story about a disagreement with a coworker, which is the BEST ending?
options: I proved my way was right and we shipped my fix.
We compared evidence, tested both approaches on staging, and shipped theirs — it handled retries better, and I said so out loud afterwards.
We argued for a while and the manager decided for us.
We avoided the topic and never discussed it again.
exercises.explain: It credits the other person, shows you work from evidence rather than ego, and ends with the working relationship intact.
exercises.hint: Who comes out of this answer looking like a good teammate?

lessons.title: The Take-Home and the End
lessons.body:
Take-homes are usually one of two things: a **case study** (here is a scenario — diagnose it and write your plan) or a **ticket-writing exercise** (here is a messy user message — write your reply). Both are graded on clarity, not cleverness.

For a ticket reply, use the shape you already know: acknowledge, show ownership, summarise, then give a next step with a time. Two or three short paragraphs beat one wall of text, and one focused question beats three.

```
Hi Dan,

Thanks for the report - I'm looking into SUP-318.

The March report totals are higher than your spreadsheet
because duplicate order IDs are being counted; I can see
14 repeats.

I'll confirm a fix time by 15:00 today.

- Aisha, Application Support
```

Then flip the table: **the questions you ask them** are half the interview. Good ones probe the day to day — how do escalations reach the engineering team, what does the first 90 days look like, how many tickets does an engineer handle in a week? Weak ones are already answered on the careers page.

Follow up with a short note within 24 hours: thank them, add the one thing you forgot to say, restate your interest. Then wait — one follow-up, not four.

exercises.prompt: Which is the BEST question to ask at the end of an Application Support interview?
options: How do escalations get from support to the engineering team?
What does your company do?
How many holiday days do employees get?
Do you enjoy working here?
exercises.explain: It asks about the day-to-day mechanics of the role — information the careers page cannot give you — and it signals you already imagine doing the job.
exercises.hint: Pick the question their website cannot answer for you.

exercises.prompt: Which is the BEST structure for a take-home ticket reply?
options: Apologise several times and promise it will never happen again
Acknowledge the issue, show ownership, summarise what you understand, and give a next step with a time
Paste the full technical log so the customer can see the detail
Ask the customer to list every piece of information they can think of
exercises.explain: The four-part shape works in a take-home exactly as it works on a live ticket: proof you read it, proof you own it, a shared understanding, and a time to come back to.
exercises.hint: Which one would you happily send to a real customer?

exercises.prompt: In the four-part ticket reply — acknowledge, show ownership, summarise — what is the fourth part?
exercises.explain: A next step with a time is what stops the user from chasing you — and it is the part most candidates leave out under exam pressure.
exercises.hint: Tell them when they will hear from you again.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps after a final interview in the correct order
items: Send a short thank-you note within 24 hours
Include the one point you forgot to make, and restate your interest
Wait until the decision date they gave you
Send one polite follow-up if that date passes
exercises.explain: One good note within a day, then patience, then a single chase — silence after that reads as pressure rather than interest.
exercises.hint: Fast, then quiet, then once.
